name: Madrid
covers: Madrid: Real Madrid and Atlético Madrid

words.means: Real Madrid's rallying cry: roughly 'Come on, Madrid!' Atleti fans never say it.
words.use: Hala Madrid! Another big European night.

words.tts: ah oo pa at let ee
words.means: Atlético's cry: 'Come on, Atleti!' The club signs off its posts with it.
words.use: Aúpa Atleti, see you at the Metropolitano.

words.means: The meringues: Real Madrid, after their all-white kit. Used by Spanish media and rival fans alike.
words.use: The merengues are top again, of course.

words.means: The Madrid derby, Real against Atlético. Spanish spells it with an i.
words.use: Derbi on Saturday. Whose side is your boss on?

words.means: A stunning goal. English-speaking fans use it too.
words.use: What a golazo, top corner from thirty yards.

words.means: A comeback from a big deficit. Real fans see it as a Bernabéu speciality on European nights.
words.use: Two down after the first leg? We've seen remontadas before.

words.means: When the crowd waves white handkerchiefs in protest at the team, the coach or the president. The worst verdict a home crowd can give.
words.use: Lose again and it'll be a pañolada.

words.means: A round of whistling. Spanish crowds whistle where English ones boo.
words.use: Big pitada for the referee at half-time.

words.means: The Champions League. Spaniards just say 'la Champions'.
words.use: Forget the league, it's all about la Champions.

words.means: A cat: a born-and-bred madrileño whose parents and grandparents were born in the city too. Said with pride.
words.use: He's a proper gato, been going to the derbi since he was five.

words.means: A small draught beer, the unit of Madrid's pre-match bar crawl.
words.use: Unas cañas near the ground before kick-off?

pronounce.why: Real's ground, officially just 'Bernabéu' since 2025. Outsiders say 'BER-na-bow'; the end runs 'bay-oo'.
Locals soften the final d almost to a 'th' (the city jokes about it as 'Madriz'). A hard English d sounds foreign.
The fountain where Real celebrate titles. The c is a 'th' in Madrid, not 'sigh-BEELZ'.
Neptune's fountain, where Atlético celebrate. Use the Spanish name, not 'Neptune'.
Real's training ground. The v is said as a soft b.
The district around the Bernabéu, often used to mean Real Madrid itself. Stress the end.

lines.t: Hala Madrid! Cibeles tonight.
lines.m: A Real fan after a trophy: the party heads to the fountain.

lines.t: Cibeles is theirs, Neptuno is ours.
lines.m: An Atleti fan on where each club celebrates.

lines.t: Derbi week. This city is split down the middle.
lines.m: Madrid is not all Real: families and offices divide.

lines.t: The Bernabéu got the hankies out again.
lines.m: Moaning about a pañolada: the crowd's patience has run out.

lines.t: Unas cañas before the game?
lines.m: The pre-match invite: small beers in a bar near the ground.

lines.t: Never leave early. Remontada.
lines.m: Real fans' faith in the late comeback.

avoid.why: They left the Vicente Calderón in 2017 and it has been demolished.

avoid.instead: Madrid is split, and Atleti have a huge local following
avoid.why: Plenty of madrileños are colchoneros and will tell you so.

avoid.say: Let's celebrate at Cibeles in red and white
avoid.why: Each club has its own fountain on the Paseo del Prado, a few hundred metres apart.

habits: Title parties end at the fountains on the Paseo del Prado: Real at Cibeles, where the captains drape the statue in a scarf, Atlético at Neptuno.
Pre-match means cañas and tapas in bars around the ground; evening kick-offs can be as late as 9pm, so dinner comes after.
Anger comes as whistles (a pitada) or, at its worst, white handkerchiefs waved at the president's box.

name: Barcelona

words.means: A Barça fan; 'culé' in Spanish. From 'cul', backside: early fans sat on the ground's wall with their behinds to the street.
words.use: Lifelong culer. My dad took me to my first Clàssic.

words.means: Catalan for 'Come on, Barça!' The everyday sign-off among fans.
words.use: Big one tonight. Força Barça!

words.means: Catalan for 'long live', as in 'Visca el Barça'. The v sounds like a b in Barcelona.
words.use: Visca el Barça! What a win.

words.means: 'More than a club': the motto painted on the stands. Fans quote it with pride; rivals quote it with a smirk.
words.use: Més que un club, mate. It's a way of life.

words.means: An official supporters' club. There are well over a thousand worldwide, and they meet in a bar to watch games.
words.use: Watching it with the penya down the road.

words.means: A club member. Barça is owned by its socis, who elect the president.
words.use: The socis vote for a new president next month.

words.means: Barça's youth academy, named after the old farmhouse that housed it. A home-grown player is 'from La Masia'.
words.use: Another kid from La Masia. Unbelievable touch.

words.means: Barça against Real Madrid; 'el Clásico' in Spanish.
words.use: Clàssic week. Nobody here talks about anything else.

words.means: Parakeets: fans of Espanyol, the city's other club, now based in Cornellà.
words.use: The pericos will be up for the derby.

words.tts: dare bee bar suh loo nee
words.means: The Barcelona derby, Barça against Espanyol.
words.use: Derbi barceloní on Saturday. Should be tasty.

words.means: Short, quick passing football. English fans use it for the Barça style; purists prefer 'positional play'.
words.use: Pure tiki-taka for ten minutes, then a tap-in.

pronounce.why: 'New field' in Catalan. Never 'the Nou Camp', and 'Nou' is not 'noo'.
In Catalan the c is an s. The 'Barthelona' lisp is Madrid Spanish, not local.
The hill with the Olympic stadium, Barça's home from 2023 to 2025. The j is soft and the end is 'eek'.
The district around the Camp Nou, and the name of the club's old ground.
The founder, and the name of Barça's pre-season trophy. Joan is a man's name in Catalan: 'zhoo-AN', not 'Jone'.
The fountain at the top of La Rambla where fans gather after titles.

lines.t: Força Barça! Canaletes if we win it.
lines.m: A fan before a title decider: the party spot is the fountain on La Rambla.

lines.t: Back at the Camp Nou, even half-built.
lines.m: Barça returned in November 2025 while the rebuild carries on.

lines.t: That's a Masia kid, you can tell.
lines.m: Praise for a home-grown player's touch.

lines.t: Clàssic week. Nobody in this city talks about anything else.
lines.m: Real Madrid week takes over Barcelona.

lines.t: The pericos? Fine, but this city is blaugrana.
lines.m: Mild banter about Espanyol, the city's other club.

avoid.why: Catalan has no 'th'; locals speaking Catalan say it with an s.
Catalan is its own language, and it's the language of the club's announcements and fan cries.

avoid.instead: Espanyol are the city's other club
avoid.why: Barcelona has two top-flight clubs and a real derby.

habits: Titles are celebrated at the Canaletes fountain at the top of La Rambla; when building work closed it in 2026, fans gathered in Plaça de Catalunya.
Many culers watch with their local penya, the official supporters' clubs found in towns across Catalonia and abroad.
The socis own the club and vote for the president; more than 100,000 were called to vote in March 2026.
unsure: pronounce: Canaletes IPA built from Catalan spelling rules, not found in a dictionary

name: Bilbao

words.means: Basque for 'come on!' and also an everyday 'hi'. 'Aupa Athletic!' is the cry.
words.use: Aupa! See you at the ground.

words.means: Basque for 'the Lions', the players' nickname. In Spanish, 'los Leones'.
words.use: The Lehoiak need a win tonight.

words.means: Basque for 'the red-and-whites': the team, and the fans in their striped shirts.
words.use: Whole city in zuri-gorri today.

words.means: Cod. What Bilbao's Radio Popular shouts instead of 'gol' when Athletic score, since 1984. Fans copy it.
words.use: Bacalao! Bacalao! One-nil.

words.means: The cubs: players in Bilbao Athletic, the reserve side. You're a cub until your first-team debut, then a lion.
words.use: Two cachorros on the bench today.

words.means: The quarry: the youth system. Athletic field only players born or trained in the Basque Country, so the cantera is everything.
words.use: All cantera, no big signings, and we won the cup.

words.means: La Liga's top-scorer award, named after an Athletic striker of the 1910s. Locals are proud it's theirs.
words.use: Fancy him for the Pichichi this year?

words.means: 'The hole': Bilbao's nickname, because the city sits in a bowl of hills. A local is a 'botxero'.
words.use: Nothing beats a derby night in the Botxo.

words.means: Basque for 'bye', used by everyone in Bilbao, even mid-Spanish.
words.use: Agur, see you Sunday.

words.means: Going bar to bar for small glasses of wine. The standard pre-match warm-up.
words.use: Poteo round Pozas at five?

words.means: The snacks lined up on Basque bar counters. 'Tx' is said 'ch'.
words.use: Couple of pintxos and then up to San Mamés.

words.means: The fine drizzle Bilbao is known for, from the Basque 'zirimiri'.
words.use: Bit of sirimiri. Proper football weather.

pronounce.why: Athletic's ground, 'La Catedral'. Stress the last syllable; not 'MAH-mez'.
Locals say the club's English name the Spanish way, stress at the front, and don't add 'Bilbao'.
Three clear syllables locally, not a clipped 'bil-BOW'.
Athletic's training ground and academy, where the cantera is raised. The z is a 'th'.
The province around Bilbao (Vizcaya in Spanish, Biscay in English). The Basque spelling is what you'll see on signs.

lines.t: Aupa! Poteo round Pozas before kick-off?
lines.m: The meet-up: bar-hopping in the streets by San Mamés.

lines.t: Bacalao! Bacalao!
lines.m: Shouted for an Athletic goal, the way local radio calls it.

lines.t: Sirimiri again. Perfect San Mamés weather.
lines.m: Fond moaning about Bilbao's drizzle.

lines.t: Basque lads only, and we still win trophies.
lines.m: Pride in the home-grown policy.

lines.t: Get the gabarra out!
lines.m: After a trophy: time for the barge parade down the river.

avoid.why: In Bilbao the bar snacks are pintxos, and the word marks who's local.

avoid.say: Basque is a kind of Spanish
avoid.instead: Basque, Euskara, is its own language
avoid.why: It's unrelated to Spanish; fans mix Basque words like aupa and agur into their Spanish.

avoid.say: Athletic should buy a star striker
avoid.instead: Athletic bring players through the cantera
avoid.why: The club only fields players born or trained in the Basque Country, and fans love it that way.

habits: Before home games, thousands do the poteo, wine and pintxos bar to bar, in the Pozas streets beside the stadium.
Visiting teams on their first trip to San Mamés lay flowers at the bust of Pichichi by the tunnel, a custom since 1927.
Trophies sail down the river on the gabarra barge; the 2024 Copa del Rey parade drew crowds put at up to a million.

name: Seville

words.means: 'My soul' said the Seville way (alma becomes arma). A warm 'mate' or 'love', very Sevillian.
words.use: Calm down, mi arma, it's only the first half.

words.means: Short for 'chiquillo', kid: the Andalusian 'mate' or 'oi'. Often cut to 'illo'.
words.use: Quillo, did you see that goal?

words.means: The Seville derby, Sevilla against Betis. One of Spain's fiercest.
words.use: Gran Derbi on Sunday. I can't sleep.

words.tts: beh teekoh ohseh bee yees tah
words.means: 'Betis or Sevilla?' The first thing a Sevillano asks you. There is no neutral answer.
words.use: So, bético o sevillista?

words.means: Old Spanish for football (ball-foot), kept in Real Betis Balompié's full name.
words.use: Real Betis Balompié. Even the name is old school.

words.means: Shouted with every pass when your team keeps the ball and the other side chases shadows.
words.use: Olé! Olé! Keep it, keep it.

words.means: The April Fair: a week of tents, dancing and late nights that takes over the city.
words.use: Home game in Feria week? Good luck getting anyone there.

words.means: Amazed, blown away: 'estoy flipando'. Sevillanos add 'en colores' when it's really big.
words.use: That comeback? I'm still flipando.

pronounce.why: The club always goes by the Spanish name. The double l is a 'y', not 'se-VIL-a'.
Sevilla's ground. The j is a breathy h, and many Sevillanos say the z as an s.
Betis's home, being rebuilt. V is a soft b and ll is a y.
The Olympic stadium by the river where Betis play while the Villamarín is rebuilt. The j is an h.
Sevilla's neighbourhood, hence 'los nervionenses'. Stress the end.
Betis's neighbourhood around the Villamarín. The h is silent.

lines.t: Bético o sevillista? Pick one, mi arma.
lines.m: Seville's first question for anyone new.

lines.t: Gran Derbi week. The whole city's on edge.
lines.m: Sevilla against Betis takes over everything.

lines.t: Quillo, what a goal!
lines.m: Andalusian 'mate' plus pure joy.

lines.t: Forty degrees and a five o'clock kick-off. Who planned this?
lines.m: Moaning about Seville's heat at early and late-season games.

lines.t: Olé! Let them chase it.
lines.m: When your side is passing rings round the opponents.

avoid.say: The Seville derby's a friendly one
avoid.why: It's one of Spain's most heated rivalries, and families split over it.
Nobody here is both; saying so gets you laughed at by each side.
Many Sevillanos say an s where Madrid says 'th', so the lisp sounds imported.

habits: Spring belongs to Semana Santa processions and the Feria de Abril; locals plan games, trips and nights out around them.
Sevilla home games open with the whole ground roaring out the club's 2005 centenary anthem, the 'Himno del Centenario'.
Betis fans head to La Cartuja by the river until the rebuilt Benito Villamarín opens, now planned for about 2028.
unsure: words: 'flipando' confirmed as Sevilla slang by one travel source plus general Spanish usage only

name: Valencia

words.means: Valencian for 'up!': the club's battle cry, as in 'Amunt València'. Also the name of the bat mascot.
words.use: Amunt València! Three points.

words.means: Valencian for 'hey' or 'mate', often spelled 'che'. It's why the club is called 'los Che'.
words.use: Xe, what a night at Mestalla.

words.means: A Valencia CF fan.
words.use: Three generations of valencianistas in my family.

words.means: Valencian for bat. The bat sits on the crest and the city's coat of arms; Spanish speakers say 'murciélago'.
words.use: Ratpenat on the shirt, ratpenat on the town hall.

words.means: The frogs: Levante, the city's other club, whose old ground sat by the riverbed.
words.use: Derbi with the granotes on Sunday.

words.tts: el soob ma ree no ah ma ree yo
words.means: The Yellow Submarine: Villarreal, the nearby town club and regional rival.
words.use: The Submarino are flying again this year.

words.means: The March festival ('Fallas' in Spanish): giant satirical figures, fireworks, and their burning on the last night.
words.use: Home game in Falles week. Bring earplugs.

words.means: The deafening daytime firecracker barrage held at 2pm every day from 1 to 19 March in the town-hall square.
words.use: Mascletà at two, Mestalla at nine.

pronounce.why: Spain's oldest top-flight ground. The double l is a 'y'-like sound, not 'mes-TAL-a'.
The new stadium, due to open in summer 2027. 'Nou' is Valencian for new.
The Valencian name, with a v and an s; the Spanish 'ba-LEN-thya' sounds different.
The city's other club. Outsiders say 'luh-VAN-tee'.
The rival town club. Four syllables, not 'VILL-a-real'.

lines.t: Amunt València!
lines.m: The cry: 'Up Valencia!'

lines.t: Xe, what a night at Mestalla.
lines.m: Valencian 'hey' after a big home win.

lines.t: Derbi with the granotes on Sunday.
lines.m: Valencia against Levante, the city derby.

lines.t: Enjoy old Mestalla while it lasts.
lines.m: The club is due to move to the Nou Mestalla in summer 2027.

lines.t: Falles week: mascletà at two, football at nine.
lines.m: March in Valencia, when fireworks and football share the day.

avoid.instead: Valencian paella: chicken, rabbit and beans
avoid.why: Paella is Valencia's own dish and locals are fierce about the recipe.

avoid.say: Levante are the new club in town
avoid.instead: Levante are older than Valencia CF
avoid.why: Levante date from 1909, ten years before Valencia CF, and their fans like saying so.

habits: In March the Falles festival fills the city: the mascletà shakes the town-hall square every afternoon and home games are played around it.
The bat, the ratpenat, is everywhere: on the crest, as the mascot Amunt, and on the city's coat of arms.
Fans are counting down their last seasons at old Mestalla before the move to the Nou Mestalla.
unsure: avoid: the paella rule is well known locally but not confirmed in a second written source during this research

name: Milan

words.means: A fan; plural 'tifosi'. A tifoso of Milan is a milanista, of Inter an interista.
words.use: He's been a tifoso since the eighties.

words.means: The curved end behind the goal where the loudest fans stand. At San Siro, Milan's is the Curva Sud and Inter's the Curva Nord.
words.use: The Curva was unreal tonight.

words.means: Milanese for 'braggart': the old nickname for Inter fans, once the posh club. Milan fans were 'casciavid', screwdrivers, the workers.
words.use: The bauscia are unbearable after a derby win.

words.means: The little golden statue of Mary on top of the Duomo, Milan's symbol. The derby is the 'Derby della Madonnina'.
words.use: Madonnina derby on Sunday. Can't wait.

words.tts: dare bee meh neh ghee no
words.means: Another name for the Milan derby. 'Meneghino' means Milanese, from the city's traditional comic character.
words.use: Derby meneghino: the city stops.

words.means: The Serie A title, after the little shield champions wear on their shirts.
words.use: The Scudetto's coming back to Milan.

words.means: The star sewn above the badge for every ten league titles. Inter have two; Milan have one.
words.use: Two stars on the shirt now. Count them.

words.means: 'Come on!' or 'Up the...': 'Forza Milan', 'Forza Inter'. The everyday sign-off.
words.use: Forza Inter, see you at San Siro.

pronounce.why: Italians call the club 'il Milan', keeping the English spelling, with the stress at the front. The city is Milano.
San Siro's official name is Stadio Giuseppe Meazza. The double z is 'ts'.
Milan's cathedral and the square where titles are celebrated. Two syllables, not 'doo-OH-mo'.
AC Milan's training ground, outside the city. Stress the 'NEL'.

pronounce.tts: ap yah no jen tee leh
pronounce.why: The town where Inter train. The final e is said.
The canal district full of bars. The 'gli' is a soft 'lyee'; the g is silent.

lines.t: Derby week. Half the office isn't talking to the other half.
lines.m: Milan and Inter split families and workplaces.

lines.t: Can't see the far Curva in this fog.
lines.m: Milan's winter fog, the city's classic weather moan.

lines.t: Aperitivo on the Navigli, then San Siro?
lines.m: The plan before an evening game.

lines.t: You've got two stars. We've got seven European Cups.
lines.m: A Milan fan's comeback when Inter fans brag about league titles.

lines.t: Enjoy San Siro while it lasts.
lines.m: The clubs bought the stadium in 2025 and plan a new one next door for the early 2030s.

avoid.say: Milan's the workers' club and Inter's the posh one
avoid.why: Supporting either club is a family matter now, and fans of both will tell you so.
It's named after the little gilded statue on the Duomo, not the singer or a church.

avoid.say: Milan and Inter have different stadiums
avoid.why: Same ground, opposite ends: Curva Sud for Milan, Curva Nord for Inter.

habits: Both clubs share San Siro: Milan's ultras fill the Curva Sud, Inter's the Curva Nord.
Titles are celebrated in Piazza del Duomo, under the Madonnina.
Before an evening game: an aperitivo in town, then the metro out to San Siro.
unsure: words: 'bauscia' is confirmed as the historic Inter nickname; current use is banter-level and not measured

name: Turin

words.means: Piedmontese for 'Madam': Turin's own nickname for Juventus, alongside 'la Vecchia Signora'.
words.use: La Madama's top of the table again.

words.tts: la fee dant sah ta dee tal ya
words.means: 'Italy's sweetheart': Juve, the club with fans all over the country, many from families who moved north to work at Fiat.
words.use: Fidanzata d'Italia: you'll find juventini in every town.

words.means: 'The hunchbacks': rivals' teasing name for Juve fans, from the baggy shirts of the 1950s that puffed up at the back. Some juventini wear it with pride.
words.use: The gobbi win again. Of course they do.

words.means: 'The Bull': Torino, the city's other club, in maroon ('granata'). Founded by players who broke away from Juve.
words.use: The Toro fans never let us forget they're the real Turin club.

words.tts: dare bee dell a moll eh
words.means: The Turin derby, Juve against Torino, named after the Mole Antonelliana, the spire on the city's skyline.
words.use: Derby della Mole Saturday. No excuses.

words.means: Juve against Inter: the 'derby of Italy' between the two clubs that most often fight for the title.
words.use: Derby d'Italia next week. The whole country will be watching.

words.means: The Serie A title, after the little shield champions wear on their shirts. Juve have won more than anyone.
words.use: Another Scudetto would do nicely.

words.means: What Italian players and fans call the head coach, borrowed from English.
words.use: The mister has to change something at half-time.

pronounce.why: The j is a 'y' and the end is 'toos'. Short form Juve: 'YOO-veh'.
The city's Italian name and the other club. Stress the middle.

pronounce.tts: moll eh an toe nell ya na
pronounce.why: The landmark that names the derby. 'Mole' has two syllables.
Juve's headquarters and training centre, next to the stadium.
The Fiat family who have owned Juve for a century. The 'gn' is 'ny'.

lines.t: Derby della Mole this weekend. The Toro will be up for it.
lines.m: Torino always raise their game for the derby.

lines.t: Love us or hate us, nobody's neutral on Juve.
lines.m: Juve have fans everywhere in Italy, and plenty of people who can't stand them.

lines.t: Call us gobbi if you like. Count the Scudetti.
lines.m: A juventino's reply to the rivals' nickname.

lines.t: Derby d'Italia: the whole country's watching.
lines.m: Juve against Inter, the big one.

lines.t: The mister needs to sort the midfield out.
lines.m: Moaning about the coach, Italian style, without naming names.

avoid.why: The city's other club uses the Italian name.

avoid.say: Juve play at the Delle Alpi
avoid.instead: Juve play at the Allianz Stadium
avoid.why: They left the Stadio delle Alpi in 2006; the new ground opened on its site in 2011.

avoid.say: Calling a Juve fan a gobbo
avoid.why: It's the rivals' teasing word. Leave it to them.

habits: Juve's support is national: families who moved north to work at Fiat made it 'Italy's sweetheart', while Torino stayed the city's own club.
The derby takes its name from the Mole Antonelliana, the tall spire that is Turin's symbol.
unsure: pronounce: Continassa and Agnelli IPA follow Italian spelling rules, not a dictionary entry

name: Rome

words.means: Roman for 'come on!', 'let's go!' or 'yes!'. 'E daje!' is pure celebration. Fans of both clubs use it.
words.use: Daje! Three points!

words.means: Roman for 'here we go again', when the same bad thing happens twice. The local moan.
words.use: Another late goal conceded. Aridaje.

words.means: Roman for 'wow!' or 'blimey!'.
words.use: Ammazza, what a strike.

words.means: Teasing banter between rival fans. After a Rome derby the sfottò goes on for days.
words.use: The sfottò at work tomorrow will be brutal.

words.means: Roma's end of the Olimpico. Lazio's fans have the Curva Nord at the other end.
words.use: Season ticket in the Curva Sud since I was ten.

words.means: Fan support; in English, the giant choreographed displays fans hold up before big games. Rome's derby tifos are famous.
words.use: Did you see the tifo before kick-off?

words.tts: dare bee dell koo po low neh
words.means: A Roman name for the derby: 'the big dome' is St Peter's. Also called the Derby della Capitale.
words.use: Derby del Cupolone: winner owns the city for six months.

words.tts: roh mah nees tah oh laht tsyah leh
words.means: 'Roma or Lazio?' The question every Roman asks. There's no third answer.
words.use: So, romanista o laziale?

pronounce.why: Named after the region around Rome. The z is 'ts'; not 'LAY-zee-oh'.
Roma's training centre. 'Trigoria' in the news means the club itself.
Lazio's training centre, north of the city.
The working-class district where Roma played early on. The 'cc' is 'ch'.
The old bridge and bar district near the Olimpico. Both words end in a clear vowel.

lines.t: Daje!
lines.m: Roman 'come on!' or 'yes!'; works for either club.

lines.t: Aridaje. Same mistakes every week.
lines.m: The Roman 'here we go again'.

lines.t: Derby week. Nobody in Rome talks about anything else.
lines.m: Roma against Lazio takes over the city.

lines.t: Ammazza, what a goal!
lines.m: Roman 'wow' after a stunner.

lines.t: The sfottò starts the morning after the derby.
lines.m: The teasing between the two sets of fans is part of the fun.

avoid.say: Roma and Lazio have their own stadiums
avoid.why: Same ground, opposite ends: Curva Sud for Roma, Curva Nord for Lazio.

avoid.instead: Lazio is the region around Rome
avoid.why: The club is from Rome itself and takes the region's name.

avoid.say: Romanista and laziale, same thing really
avoid.why: The rivalry is about who owns the city, and nobody is both.

habits: Both clubs share the Stadio Olimpico, and on derby day the Curva Sud and Curva Nord face each other with tifos planned for weeks.
The sfottò, teasing banter, carries on at work, in bars and online for days after a derby.
Fans meet in the bars around Ponte Milvio and walk to the Olimpico.
unsure: words: 'sfottò' IPA from Italian spelling (Wiktionary gives none)
habits: Ponte Milvio as the pre-match meeting spot is from general knowledge, not a second source

name: Naples

words.means: 'Come on, Napoli!' Often finished with 'sempre', always.
words.use: Forza Napoli, sempre.

words.means: Neapolitan for a lad or boy. Shouted as 'guagliò!' to a mate or a player.
words.use: Guagliò, what a goal!

words.means: A Naples street kid. Said fondly of a cheeky, streetwise player.
